en: Points of Controversy Great Fifty-Section Second Chapter
The Discourse on Doubt:
Is there doubt for an Arahant?
Yes, [you say].
Is there doubt, the obsession of doubt, the fetter of doubt, and the hindrance of doubt in an Arahant?
One should not say so… [as before] … Is it not the case that there is no doubt, no obsession of doubt, no fetter of doubt, and no hindrance of doubt in an Arahant?
“Yes.
“If it is true that for an Arahant there is no doubt, no obsession by doubt, no fetter of doubt, and no hindrance of doubt, then surely you should not say:
‘An Arahant has perplexity.’”
An ordinary person has doubt; does he have perplexity, the obsession of perplexity, the fetter of perplexity, and the hindrance of perplexity?
Yes. Does an Arahant have doubt; does he have perplexity, the obsession of perplexity, the fetter of perplexity, and the hindrance of perplexity? No.
It should not be said so … [as before] … Does an Arahant have doubt? No. Has he perplexity, the obsession of perplexity, the fetter of perplexity, or the hindrance of perplexity?
Yes.
An ordinary person has doubt; does he not have perplexity, the obsession of perplexity, the fetter of perplexity, and the hindrance of perplexity?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Does an Arahant have doubt?
“Yes,” [you say]. “Does an arahant have doubt regarding the Teacher, doubt regarding the Dhamma, doubt regarding the Saṅgha, doubt regarding the training,
doubt regarding the past, doubt regarding the future, doubt regarding both the past and the future, or doubt regarding specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena?”
It should not be said so.

Is it not the case that for an Arahant there is no doubt regarding the Teacher, no doubt regarding the Dhamma, and [so on] … no doubt regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions?
Yes, it is.

If there is no doubt in an Arahant regarding the Teacher, nor doubt regarding the Dhamma, nor even doubt regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions, then surely it should not be said:
“An Arahant has doubt.

But does an ordinary person (puthujjana) have doubt? Does he have doubt regarding the Teacher, doubt regarding the Dhamma, and so on, up to doubt regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then does an arahant have doubt? Does he have doubt regarding the Teacher, doubt regarding the Dhamma …pe… doubt regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions?
One should certainly not say so.

Does an Arahant have doubt? He has no doubt regarding the Teacher, no doubt regarding the Dhamma, ... [and so on] ... no doubt regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions?

Yes. Does an ordinary person have doubt? He has no doubt regarding the Teacher, no doubt regarding the Dhamma, ... [and so on] ... no doubt regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions?
It should not be said so.
Is there doubt in an Arahant? Yes.
Is it not the case that for an Arahant, lust has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future?
Yes, it is.

If for an Arahant lust has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future, then indeed, you should not say: [that the Arahant still possesses lust].
“There is doubt in an Arahant.
Is there doubt in an Arahant?
Yes, [you say].
Is it not the case that for an Arahant, hatred has been abandoned … pe … delusion has been abandoned … pe … moral shamelessness has been abandoned … pe …?
The path has been developed for the abandoning of lust … [and] the factors of enlightenment have been developed … [likewise] for the abandoning of hatred … etc.
The path has been developed for the abandoning of fearlessness of wrongdoing …pe… the factors of enlightenment have been developed;
is not the Arahant one who is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion …pe…?
Is that which is to be realized realized? Yes.
If so, then the Arahant is one who is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion... [and so forth].
That which is to be realized has been realized; indeed, one should not say, "There is doubt in the Arahant.
Is there doubt in the Arahant?
"An arahant skilled in his own doctrine has doubt; an arahant skilled in another's doctrine has no doubt.
[Query: "Does an arahant skilled in his own doctrine have doubt? [Response:
"Yes."
Does the Arahant who is skilled in other doctrines have doubt?
One should not say so … [as before] … Does the Arahant who is skilled in other doctrines not have doubt?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does an Arahant skilled in the True Dhamma have no doubt?
You should not say so …pe….
Is doubt present in an arahant who is skilled in his own Dhamma, even though lust has been abandoned by him?
Yes. Is doubt present in an arahant who is skilled in another’s Dhamma, even though lust has been abandoned by him? Yes.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … For an Arahant skilled in his own doctrine,
hatred has been abandoned … delusion has been abandoned … [as before].
Fearlessness of wrongdoing has been abandoned … the path for the abandonment of lust has been developed … the factors of enlightenment have been developed … [and so on].
The path has been developed for the abandoning of hatred …pe… for the abandoning of delusion …pe… for the abandoning of lack of moral dread …pe…
When the factors of enlightenment have been developed … [as before] … an arahant who is skilled in his own Dhamma, free from lust, free from hatred,
and free from delusion … [as before] … has realized what was to be realized; does he still have doubt?
“Yes. “Then,
is there doubt in that Arahant— who is skilled in others’ doctrines, free from lust, free from hatred,
and free from delusion … [and who has] realized what is to be realized?”
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is passion abandoned by an Arahant who is skilled in other doctrines, and does he have no doubt? Yes.
Is lust abandoned by an Arahant who is skilled in his own Dhamma, and does he have no doubt?
One should not say so …pe….
Is hatred abandoned by an Arahant who is skilled in another’s Dhamma …pe….
Delusion has been abandoned … [and so on] … lack of moral dread has been abandoned … [and so on] … the path for the abandoning of lust has been developed … [and so on].
The factors of enlightenment,
when developed … lead to the abandoning of hatred … lead to the abandoning of delusion … lead to the abandoning of [all] defilements.
The path has been developed for the abandoning of fearlessness of wrongdoing … the factors of enlightenment have been developed … [and] one who is skilled in the doctrines of others is an arahant,
free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion … [and so forth].
“Has what ought to be realized been realized by him, so that there is no doubt for him?
“Yes.
“An Arahant who is skilled in his own Dhamma, free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion … [as before] …”
"Is that which is to be realized already realized, such that for him there is no doubt?
One should not say so... [etc.
... "Does the Arahant have doubt?"
“Yes, [it is so].
“Is it not stated by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see’?”
And what, bhikkhus, is it that one who knows and sees thus experiences the destruction of the taints?
‘Such is form,’ ...pe...
‘such is the passing away of consciousness.’”
“It is for one who knows thus, bhikkhus, and for one who sees thus, that the destruction of the taints occurs.
Is this indeed a sutta? Yes.
In that case, it should not be said:
"There is doubt in an Arahant.
Is there doubt in an Arahant?
“Yes, [it is so].
“Is it not stated by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see’?”
And what, bhikkhus, is it that one who knows and sees thus has the destruction of the taints?
"This is suffering," bhikkhus... [as before] ...
"This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering"—for one who knows and sees thus, there is the destruction of the taints.
“Thus, monks, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the destruction of the taints.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
In that case, it should not be said:
"There is doubt in the Arahant.
Is there doubt in the Arahant?
“Yes, [it is so].
“Is it not stated by the Blessed One:
‘Bhikkhus, without directly knowing, without fully understanding, without becoming dispassionate toward, and without abandoning everything, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering’?”
“Indeed, monks, by directly knowing and fully understanding everything, by fading away from it and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
In that case, it should not be said:
"An arahant has doubt. Does an arahant have doubt?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “Is it not said by the Blessed One:
‘With the attainment of vision for him...’?”
“The six impossibilities cannot be done.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
In that case, it should not be said:
"There is doubt in an Arahant.
Is there doubt in an Arahant?
“Yes, [it is so].
“Was it not said by the Blessed One:
‘Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arises in a noble disciple—’?”
“‘Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation’—with the arising of this vision, bhikkhus, three fetters are abandoned in a noble disciple:
personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
Is there such a sutta?
“Yes.
In that case, it should not be said:
“An arahant has doubt.”
"Does doubt exist for an arahant?
"Yes.
"But was it not said by the Blessed One:"
“When, indeed, phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts vanish away.”
"Because he understands phenomena together with their causes.
When phenomena indeed become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin;
Then all his doubts vanish,
since he has understood the destruction of conditions.
When phenomena indeed become manifest...
For the brahmin who meditates with ardor,
dispelling the army of Māra,
he stands like the sun illuminating the sky.
Whatever doubt there may be here or in the world beyond,
whether to be experienced by oneself or by another—
all that the meditators abandon.
"Exerting themselves, living the holy life":
those who have transcended doubt regarding beings who are subject to doubt.
Free from doubt and detached,
what is given to them bears great fruit.
Such is the proclamation of the Dhamma here.
No disciple there has any doubt;
we pay homage to the Buddha, the Conqueror, the Lord of Men, who has crossed the flood and severed all uncertainty.
Is it indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said—
“An arahant has doubt.
Should one not say,
“An arahant has doubt”?
“Yes.

“But would an arahant have doubt regarding the names and clans of men and women? Would he have doubt regarding what is the path and what is not the path? Would he have doubt regarding the names of grasses, sticks, and trees?
“Yes.”
If an Arahant were to doubt the names and clans of men and women, or doubt what is the path and what is not the path, or doubt the names of grasses,
sticks, and trees, then indeed, sir,
one could say of him: "The Arahant has doubt."

If one were to say: "An Arahant might doubt the names and clans of men and women; he might doubt what is the path and what is not the path; he might doubt the names of grasses, wood, and forest trees"—is there doubt for an Arahant? Yes.
[Then] would an Arahant doubt the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or Arahantship itself?
It should not be stated thus... [etc.
...The Discussion on Doubt is finished.
